title: Birds: how beaks and feet fit their food, and why birds are dinosaurs

summary.text: A beak can crack a seed or sip nectar, and scientists say birds are dinosaurs. What shows that? In this unit you will watch a bird's beak and feet, test where a beak bites hardest with a lever, match clue cards, and find the dinosaur in a bird.
summary.art: A house sparrow cracking a seed on a wall and a long-beaked godwit probing wet mud, with the faint outline of a small feathered dinosaur behind them.

intro.hook: A sparrow's beak is short and thick. A godwit's beak is as long as a pencil. Why can the sparrow crack a hard seed when the godwit cannot?
intro.text: A beak has two halves joined at a hinge, like a pair of scissors. In this unit you cut stacks of newspaper with scissors, near the hinge and at the tips. You find out which part cuts hardest and which part reaches farthest. That explains why birds with different foods have different beaks. Then you read feet, nests and migration in the same way. Last, you look for a dinosaur's features on a bird at your window.
intro.art: A child's hand holding a pair of scissors over a folded stack of newspaper, with a sparrow and a godwit drawn on a notebook page beside it.

outcomes: I can look at a beak and say what food that beak fits, and why.
I can explain why a short, deep beak bites harder than a long, thin beak.
I can match perching, climbing, paddling, wading and grasping feet to the way a bird lives.
I can describe four kinds of nest and say what problem each one solves.
I can explain why some birds migrate, and name two birds who spend the winter in India.
I can give four features that birds share with small meat-eating dinosaurs.
I can tell how scientists found out that birds are dinosaurs, and name one idea that was wrong.
I can explain how a drought changed the beaks of finches within a few years.

terms.meaning: The hard mouth of a bird. It is made of bone with a covering of keratin, the material of your fingernails. Another word for beak is bill.
terms.example: A parakeet's beak is short and hooked. A kingfisher's beak is long and straight.
terms.art: A rose-ringed parakeet and a white-throated kingfisher side by side, with their beaks drawn large.

terms.meaning: A stiff bar that turns about a fixed point, called the hinge or pivot. A push near the hinge is strong, and a push far from the hinge is weak.
terms.example: Scissors are two levers. They cut thick card near the hinge and only thin paper at the tips.
terms.art: A pair of open scissors with an arrow marking the hinge and two more arrows marking a place near the hinge and a place at the tips.

terms.meaning: A long, sharp, curved claw on the foot of a bird who hunts.
terms.example: A black kite grips her prey with her talons and tears the meat with her hooked beak.
terms.art: A close view of a kite's foot with four curved talons gripping a small fish.

terms.meaning: A foot with skin stretched between the toes. It pushes a lot of water, like a paddle.
terms.example: A spot-billed duck paddles across a tank with webbed feet.
terms.art: A duck's orange foot seen from below, with the skin between the three front toes spread wide.

terms.meaning: A bird with long legs who walks in shallow water or on wet mud to find food.
terms.example: A godwit is a wader. She walks on wet mud and pushes her long beak into it.
terms.art: A long-legged brown bird with a long straight beak walking in shallow water at the edge of a marsh.

terms.meaning: A foot with three toes pointing forward and one pointing back. The toes wrap round a twig or a wire.
terms.example: A sparrow, a crow and a bulbul all have perching feet.
terms.art: A sparrow's foot wrapped round a thin wire, with three toes in front and one behind.

terms.meaning: To keep eggs warm until they hatch. Most birds do it by sitting on the eggs.
terms.example: A bulbul incubates her eggs for about two weeks.
terms.art: A red-vented bulbul sitting low in a small cup nest in a bush.

terms.meaning: A long journey that an animal makes at the same time every year, and then makes back again.
terms.example: Bar-headed geese fly from Mongolia and Tibet to India every autumn. They fly back in spring.
terms.art: A line of geese flying over high snow mountains, with a small map showing an arrow from Central Asia to India.

terms.meaning: A bird who breeds in another country and comes to India only for the cold months.
terms.example: The black-tailed godwit is a winter visitor. She nests far to the north and feeds in Indian wetlands from about October to March.
terms.art: A marsh in India in winter with many long-legged birds feeding, and a calendar strip with October to March coloured in.

terms.meaning: The remains or the mark of a living being from long ago, kept in rock.
terms.example: A fossil found in Germany in 1861 shows a bird-like animal with feathers, teeth and a long bony tail.
terms.art: A flat slab of pale stone with the dark outline of a small feathered skeleton pressed into it.

terms.meaning: A dinosaur from the group that walked on two legs and had hollow bones and three main toes. Most theropods ate meat. Birds belong to this group.
terms.example: Tyrannosaurus, Velociraptor and Rajasaurus from India were theropods. So is a hen.
terms.art: A row of four animals walking on two legs and getting smaller: Tyrannosaurus, Rajasaurus, Velociraptor and a hen.

terms.meaning: A bone shaped like the letter V at the front of the chest. It is made of the two collarbones joined together.
terms.example: A hen has a wishbone. So did Velociraptor and Tyrannosaurus.
terms.art: A thin V-shaped bone drawn beside the outline of a hen's chest, with a line pointing to the place of the bone.

terms.meaning: When the individuals whose bodies suit a place best live longer and have more young. Their features then become more common.
terms.example: In a drought, finches with deeper beaks could crack the hard seeds that were left. More of them lived, and their chicks had deeper beaks too.
terms.art: Two small finches on dry ground. One has a deeper beak and is cracking a large spiky fruit. The other has a smaller beak and is watching.

explanations.concept: A beak is a tool that fits a way of feeding
explanations.definition: A beak is the hard mouth of a bird. Its shape fits the food the bird eats and the way the bird gets that food.
explanations.description: A bird has no hands and no teeth. The beak does the work of both. It is light, because it is thin bone with a covering of keratin, the material of your fingernails. The covering keeps growing, as your nails do, and wears down with use. Different foods need different tools. A sparrow has a short, thick cone that cracks seeds. A sunbird has a long, thin, curved beak that reaches the nectar deep in a flower. A kite has a sharp hook that tears meat. A duck has a flat beak with edges like a comb, which strain small food out of water. A woodpecker has a straight chisel that cuts into bark. A godwit has a very long beak that probes soft mud for worms. A crow has a strong, straight beak of middle length, and eats almost anything. A beak also does other jobs. Birds use beaks to clean and oil their feathers, to build nests, to feed chicks and to fight.
examples: Seed cracker: house sparrow, munia, parakeet.
Nectar probe: purple sunbird.
Meat hook: black kite, barn owl.
Strainer: spot-billed duck, flamingo.
Mud probe: godwit, sandpiper.
explanations.art: Six bird heads in a row, each beside a kitchen or tool-box tool of the same shape: a nutcracker, a straw, a hook, a tea strainer, a chisel and long tweezers.

explanations.concept: A short beak bites hard, and a long beak reaches far
explanations.definition: A beak works as a pair of levers. A lever pushes hard near the hinge and weakly far from the hinge.
explanations.description: The two halves of a beak meet at a hinge at the back of the mouth. The muscles that close the beak pull near that hinge. This is the same plan as a pair of scissors. In the Beak Lever Test, scissors cut a thick stack of newspaper near the hinge. At the tips they cut only a thin stack. The muscle pulls with the same force the whole time, but the bite is not the same everywhere along the beak. Close to the hinge, the bite is strong. Far from the hinge, the bite is weak. So a short, deep beak gives a hard bite at the tip, because the tip is close to the hinge. A finch cracks her hardest seeds near the base of her beak, where the bite is strongest. A long beak has a weak bite at the tip. But the tip of a long beak moves farther and faster when the beak opens and shuts. It also reaches deep into mud, water or a flower. No beak can have the hardest bite and the longest reach together. That is why seed-crackers have short beaks and probing birds have long ones.
examples: A sparrow cracks a grain of bajra with a beak about one centimetre long.
A godwit's beak is about ten centimetres long. She uses it to reach worms, and she swallows them whole.
A kingfisher's long beak snaps shut very fast on a fish.
explanations.art: A sparrow's short beak and a godwit's long beak drawn above a pair of scissors, with the hinge marked on all three.

explanations.concept: Feet show where a bird lives and how they get food
explanations.definition: A bird's feet fit the surface the bird stands on and the way the bird catches or holds food.
explanations.description: Most small birds have perching feet. Three toes point forward and one points back, so the foot wraps round a twig. Woodpeckers, parakeets and barbets have two toes forward and two back. That grip holds on to an upright tree trunk. A parakeet also uses one foot as a hand, to hold a fruit while she bites it. Ducks have webbed feet, with skin between the toes, which push water like paddles. Herons and godwits have long legs and long toes. Long legs keep the body dry. Long toes spread the bird's weight, so she does not sink in mud. A jacana has the longest toes of all for her size, and walks on floating lotus leaves. Kites, eagles and owls have talons, which are long curved claws that grip and kill prey. A vulture has a hooked beak like an eagle's, but weak feet with blunt claws. Vultures eat animals who are already dead, so they do not need to grip prey. A hen and a peafowl have thick, strong toes that scratch the ground.
examples: Perching: sparrow, crow, bulbul.
Climbing: woodpecker, parakeet, barbet.
Paddling: duck, goose.
Wading: heron, godwit, jacana.
Grasping: kite, eagle, owl.
explanations.art: Five bird feet in a row with labels: a perching foot on a twig, a climbing foot on bark, a webbed foot, a long-toed wading foot on a leaf and a foot with talons.

explanations.concept: How a sleeping bird stays on a branch
explanations.definition: A sleeping bird's toes stay closed round a branch. A lock in the toe tendons helps, and scientists argue about how much.
explanations.description: A myna sleeps all night on a thin branch and does not fall. Part of the reason is in the tendons of the foot. A tendon is a tough cord that joins a muscle to a bone. The tendons that close a bird's toes run down the back of the leg and under the toes. The underside of each tendon has tiny bumps. The tube around the tendon has tiny ridges. When the toes close round a branch, the bumps catch on the ridges. Then the toes stay closed with little effort. Scientists agree that this lock is there. They do not agree on how much this lock matters during sleep.
examples: A parakeet hangs upside down from a wire by her feet.
A kite carries a fish in her talons for many minutes without dropping it.
In The Sleeping Grip activity, your own fingers curl when your wrist is bent back.

perspectives.who: The older view, found in many books
perspectives.explanation: When a bird squats, the bent ankle pulls the tendons tight, and the toes close by themselves. The bird's own weight keeps the lock shut all night.

perspectives.who: Peter Galton and Jeffrey Shepherd, who tested starlings in 2012
perspectives.explanation: Bending the legs of starlings did not close their toes. Sleeping starlings often stood with their toes loose and kept their balance. So the grip may be less automatic than the books say.

explanations.art: A bird's leg and foot drawn with a cord running down the back of the leg and under the toes, and a small circle showing bumps on the cord caught on ridges.

explanations.definition: Natural selection means that the individuals whose bodies suit a place best live longer and have more young. Over generations, their features become more common.
explanations.description: No two sparrows have exactly the same beak, just as no two people have the same nose. Chicks get much of their beak shape from their parents. Rosemary Grant and Peter Grant studied finches on Daphne Major, a small island in the Galápagos, from 1973. They caught, ringed and measured almost every finch. In 1977 almost no rain fell. The small, soft seeds were soon eaten. Only large, hard seeds were left. Of about 1,200 medium ground finches, only about 180 lived through the drought. The finches who lived had deeper beaks than the average finch before the drought. A deeper beak cracks a harder seed. The chicks born the next year had beaks about half a millimetre deeper than the birds before the drought. Half a millimetre is small, but it is the difference between cracking a seed and starving. No finch changed their own beak. The share of deep beaks in the flock changed. This is how beaks come to fit foods.
examples: After the 1977 drought, the finches of Daphne Major had deeper beaks.
After a very wet year in 1983, small seeds were plentiful, and finches with smaller beaks did better.
House sparrows taken to North America in the 1850s now differ in size from place to place.
explanations.art: A small dry island with a few finches, and two bar-like rows of finch heads labelled Before the drought and After the drought, the second row with slightly deeper beaks.

explanations.concept: A nest is a place built for eggs and chicks
explanations.definition: A nest is a place that a bird makes or chooses for eggs and chicks. A nest keeps them warm, dry and safe from hunters.
explanations.description: An egg must stay warm, and a chick cannot fly away from danger. Every nest is an answer to those two problems. A red-wattled lapwing lays her eggs in a shallow scrape on open ground. The eggs are speckled like the soil, so they are hard to see. A bulbul weaves a cup of thin twigs and roots in a bush. A baya weaver hangs a woven nest from the tip of a thin branch, often over water. Few snakes can climb out to such a nest. The male baya weaves the nest with his beak and feet, and the female inspects it before she accepts it. A red-rumped swallow builds a nest of mud pellets under a bridge or a roof. A great hornbill mother goes into a tree hole and seals the opening with her droppings and mud. She leaves a narrow slit, and the father passes food through it for weeks. An Asian koel builds no nest. The female lays her egg in a crow's nest, and the crows raise the chick. A nest is not a home for the whole year. Most birds use it only while there are eggs and chicks.
examples: Scrape on the ground: red-wattled lapwing.
Woven hanging nest: baya weaver.
Mud nest: red-rumped swallow.
Sealed tree hole: great hornbill.
No nest of their own: Asian koel.
explanations.art: Five small scenes: speckled eggs in a ground scrape, a cup nest in a bush, a woven nest hanging from a palm leaf, a mud nest under a bridge and a tree hole with a narrow slit and a hornbill's beak.

explanations.concept: Migration: two places in one year
explanations.definition: Migration is a long journey that an animal makes at the same time every year, and then makes back again.
explanations.description: In the far north, summer days are very long. The ground thaws, and the lakes and mud fill with insects and worms. There is enough food to raise chicks quickly. In winter the same ground freezes hard and is covered with snow. In the Frozen Mud Test, tweezers found no beans in the frozen bowl, though all ten beans were still there. A godwit in frozen country has the same problem. Her food is still in the ground, and her beak cannot reach it. So she flies south to India, where the mud stays soft. In spring she flies back north to nest. Many birds come to India for the winter. Bar-headed geese fly from Mongolia and Tibet across the Himalayas. Scientists have tracked them at more than 6,000 metres above the sea. Demoiselle cranes come to Rajasthan from Central Asia. Amur falcons rest in Nagaland each October on their way from East Asia to southern Africa. Birds find their way by the Sun, the stars, landmarks and the Earth's magnetic field. How they sense the magnetic field is still being worked out.
examples: Bar-headed goose: Mongolia and Tibet to Indian lakes.
Black-tailed godwit: Central Asia and Siberia to Indian marshes.
Demoiselle crane: Central Asia to Khichan in Rajasthan.
Amur falcon: East Asia to southern Africa, by way of Nagaland.
explanations.art: A map of Asia with four curved arrows ending in India. A goose, a godwit, a crane and a falcon are drawn where the arrows begin.

explanations.definition: Birds are the one group of dinosaurs still alive. They belong to the theropods, the dinosaurs who walked on two legs.
explanations.description: Dinosaurs first appear in rocks about 230 million years old. One group, the theropods, walked on two legs. They had hollow bones, three main toes and a wishbone. Tyrannosaurus was a theropod. So was Rajasaurus, whose bones were found in Gujarat. Some small theropods had feathers. They laid eggs with hard shells in nests, and sat on them. Fossils from Mongolia show a dinosaur called Citipati sitting on a nest. The arms are spread over the eggs, as a hen spreads her wings. Another small dinosaur, Mei long, was found curled up with the head tucked under one arm. A sleeping duck tucks her head under a wing in the same way. By about 150 million years ago, some small feathered theropods could fly. Archaeopteryx, found in Germany in 1861, had feathered wings, and also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail. About 66 million years ago a large asteroid hit the Earth. Every dinosaur died out except some of the birds. Today there are more than 10,000 kinds of birds. So a crow is as much a dinosaur as Tyrannosaurus was.
examples: A hen's scaly feet and three front toes are theropod feet.
A hen's wishbone is the same bone as the wishbone of Velociraptor.
Citipati sat on a nest of eggs, as a hen does.
explanations.art: A family tree drawn as branching lines, with a crocodile on the lowest branch, then a long-necked dinosaur, Tyrannosaurus, Velociraptor, Archaeopteryx, a hen and a sparrow at the top.

explanations.concept: Feathers came before flight, and how flight began is argued
explanations.definition: The first feathers grew on dinosaurs who could not fly. Flight came later, and scientists argue about how it began.
explanations.description: In 1996 a farmer in Liaoning, in China, found a fossil of a small theropod. The animal had a coat of short, hair-like feathers. This kind of dinosaur was named Sinosauropteryx, and lived about 125 million years ago. They had short arms and could not fly. So feathers did not begin as tools for flying. The first feathers probably kept small dinosaurs warm, and may have been used for display. Scientists have even found the colour of some feathers. Tiny grains that held the colour are kept in the fossils. Sinosauropteryx had a tail with reddish-brown and pale rings. Long wing feathers and flight came later. Scientists do not agree on how flight began.
examples: Sinosauropteryx had feathers and could not fly.
A peacock's train is made of feathers and is used for display, not for flying.
A partridge chick flaps tiny wings to run up a steep slope.

perspectives.explanation: Small feathered dinosaurs climbed trees and glided down. Gliding slowly turned into flapping flight.
Small feathered dinosaurs ran fast and leapt after prey. Feathered arms helped them leap higher and steer.

perspectives.who: Kenneth Dial, who studied partridge chicks in 2003
perspectives.explanation: Chicks who cannot yet fly flap their wings to run up steep slopes and tree trunks. Small dinosaurs may have used half-grown wings in the same way.

explanations.art: A small two-legged dinosaur covered in short reddish fuzz with a long ringed tail, standing beside a hen for size.

explanations.concept: Why only the birds lived through the asteroid
explanations.definition: Scientists have ideas, but no proof, about why some birds lived through the asteroid strike when all other dinosaurs died.
explanations.description: The asteroid that struck 66 million years ago set off fires and filled the sky with dust. Plants stopped growing for many months, and forests fell. Every large land animal died. Many kinds of birds died too, including all the birds who still had teeth. Scientists have ideas about why some birds lived, and none is proved. The birds who lived were small, so they needed little food. They had beaks without teeth, and some may have eaten seeds. Seeds stay good to eat in the soil for years after plants stop growing. Many of the birds who lived seem to have lived on the ground, which helped when the forests were gone.
examples: Seeds buried in soil can last for years.
A small body needs less food than a large one.
The birds with teeth all died out.
explanations.art: A dark, dusty landscape with fallen burnt trees, and three small ground birds pecking seeds from the soil in the foreground.

agreed.text: The shape of a beak fits what the bird eats and the way the bird feeds.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have watched what birds eat and measured their beaks in thousands of kinds of birds.

agreed.text: A beak bites hardest near the hinge, and a deeper beak bites harder.
agreed.evidence: In 2005 Anthony Herrel's team let wild Galápagos finches bite a small force meter. Finches with deeper beaks and bigger heads bit harder.

agreed.text: Beaks can change within a few years by natural selection.
agreed.evidence: Rosemary and Peter Grant measured the finches of Daphne Major every year from 1973. After the 1977 drought, the next generation had deeper beaks.
Fossils show theropods with feathers, wishbones, hollow bones, nests of eggs and bird-like sleeping poses. Dozens of kinds of feathered dinosaur have been found since 1996.

agreed.text: An asteroid strike about 66 million years ago ended all dinosaurs except birds.
agreed.evidence: In 1980 Luis Alvarez, Walter Alvarez, Frank Asaro and Helen Michel studied rocks of that age. They found a thin layer rich in iridium, a metal that is common in asteroids. The crater was later found in Mexico.

agreed.text: Many birds fly thousands of kilometres between a summer place and a winter place.
agreed.evidence: Rings on birds' legs and small trackers on their backs show the routes. Tracked bar-headed geese crossed the Himalayas at more than 6,000 metres.

challenging.who: Everyday speech and many older books
challenging.for: Tyrannosaurus, the long-necked giants and every other large dinosaur died out about 66 million years ago.
challenging.against: Birds are theropod dinosaurs, and more than 10,000 kinds are alive. The sentence is true only of the other dinosaurs.

challenging.claim: Birds cannot have come from dinosaurs, because dinosaurs had no wishbone.
challenging.who: The Danish artist and scientist Gerhard Heilmann, in a book of 1926
challenging.for: In 1926 no dinosaur wishbone had been recognised, and a lost bone was thought never to come back.
challenging.against: Wishbones have since been found in many theropods, including Velociraptor and Tyrannosaurus.

challenging.claim: You can always tell a bird's food from the beak.
challenging.for: The rule works for most birds, and the Beak Lever Test shows why.
challenging.against: A crow's plain beak takes almost any food. A toucan's huge beak is used for fruit, and also gives off body heat to cool the bird. Beaks do several jobs.

challenging.who: Most books since the fossil was found in 1861
challenging.for: Archaeopteryx had wings with flight feathers and lived about 150 million years ago.
challenging.against: Small feathered dinosaurs of about the same age have been found in China. In 2011 Xu Xing's team argued that Archaeopteryx sits beside the first birds, and not among them. Others disagree.

challenging.who: Some scientists, after a large feathered relative named Yutyrannus was found in China in 2012
challenging.for: Yutyrannus was about 9 metres long and had long, simple feathers. So a giant relative of Tyrannosaurus did have them.
challenging.against: Skin prints from Tyrannosaurus show small scales on several parts of the body. A full-grown Tyrannosaurus may have had few feathers or none.

big_questions.q: If a sparrow is a dinosaur, what should the word 'dinosaur' mean?
big_questions.hint: Should a word follow the family of the animal, or the way most people speak?

big_questions.q: A crow eats almost anything, and a sunbird mostly drinks nectar. Which way of living is safer?
big_questions.hint: Think about a year when the flowers fail, and a year when there are too many crows.

big_questions.q: The finches' beaks changed after one drought. Is any kind of animal ever finished changing?
big_questions.hint: The weather, the food and the neighbours keep changing too.

big_questions.q: A godwit spends half the year in Siberia and half in India. Which place is her home?
big_questions.hint: Ask what you mean by home: where you were born, where you eat, or where you raise your young.

big_questions.q: A young baya weaver's first nest is often untidy, and his later nests are neat. Is nest building inborn or learnt?
big_questions.hint: Could it be some of each? What would you need to watch to find out?

big_questions.q: We know Velociraptor only from bones. What could you never learn about a sparrow from bones alone?
big_questions.hint: Think of her song, her colour, and what she is afraid of.

story.title: The Long Beak on the Terrace
story.note: Kayal, her father and Shanthi are made up, and so is this godwit's landing on a terrace. These facts are real. Black-tailed godwits breed in Central Asia and Siberia and spend the winter in Indian wetlands, including marshes near Chennai. A godwit feeds by pushing her long beak deep into soft mud. The tip of the beak can feel a worm move. Bird rescuers do ask people to keep a tired wild bird in a dark box with air holes. They also ask people not to push food into the beak.
text: The storm blew over Velachery all night. In the morning the terrace was covered with neem leaves, and there was one bird.

Kayal saw her when she went up to bring down the clothes clips. The bird stood beside the water tank on legs like two thin grey sticks. She was brown, and as tall as a hen, but much slimmer. Her beak was the strange part. It was straight, pink near the face and dark at the tip, and almost as long as Kayal's hand.
The bird did not fly away. She took three steps and sat down.
"Appa!" Kayal called down the stairs. "Come and see. Come slowly."

Appa came up with the phone already in his hand. He rang the bird rescue number that was painted on the wall near the bus stop. A woman called Shanthi answered. She said that after a storm, tired birds came down in all sorts of places.

"Put her in a big box with air holes," Shanthi said. "Keep it dark and quiet. Give her a flat dish of water. Do not push food into her beak. I am in Tambaram with a hurt owl, so I can come only in the evening."

They found the box that the mixer had come in. Appa lifted the bird in a towel. She weighed almost nothing. Kayal saw her feet as they went past. Each foot had three long toes spread wide, and one small toe behind. There was no skin between the toes.
All morning Kayal sat beside the box. No sound came from it. At noon Appa could not bear it any longer.
"She must be hungry," he said. "Shanthi madam told us not to push food. She did not tell us not to offer it."

He put a spoon of raw rice in a jar lid and slid it into the box. An hour later he tried soaked chana, broken small. Then he tried a piece of banana. The bird looked at each one with a dark eye and did not move.
"Maybe she is too sick to eat," said Appa.

Kayal looked through an air hole at the long beak. She thought about the sparrows at the ration shop. They cracked spilt grain with short, fat beaks, crick, crick, like tiny nutcrackers. Then she thought about the scissors in her craft box. They cut thick card only near the screw. At the tips they could hardly cut two sheets.
"Appa, she cannot eat rice," Kayal said. "Look at her beak. It is as long as a pencil. A beak like that is weak at the tip. It cannot crack anything. It is made for reaching."
"Reaching what?"

"Something deep, and something soft." Kayal thought about the long legs and the wide, bare toes. This bird was not a swimmer, because she had no skin between her toes. She was not a tree bird either. Legs like those would be no use on a twig.
"She walks in shallow water, Appa. She walks on soft mud. She pushes that beak down into the mud for worms."
Appa laughed. "So I should cook worms."

"No. We should not feed her at all. We should take her where her food is. Not the park, as you said this morning, and not the temple tank. There is nothing for her in a tree, and the tank is deep, with stone steps. She needs mud that her beak can go into."
When Shanthi rang at four o'clock, Kayal took the phone and said all of it in one breath. For a moment Shanthi said nothing.
"A long straight beak, pink near the face?" she asked. "Long legs? Did you see white on the wing?"
"I saw white when Appa lifted her."

"Then she is a black-tailed godwit," said Shanthi. "She has flown here from far to the north, beyond the Himalayas. I think the storm brought her down before she reached the marsh. You are right about the mud. If she is standing up and holding both wings level, meet me on the Pallikaranai marsh road at five."

The marsh lay between the big road and the glass office towers. The water was low at the edges, and the mud shone. Shanthi looked at the bird's wings and eyes, and nodded. Kayal opened the flap of the box and stepped back.

For a long moment the godwit did nothing. Then she walked out, lifting her feet high. Her wide toes did not sink. At the edge of the water she put her head down and pushed her beak into the mud, right up to her face. She did it again and again, as fast as the needle of a sewing machine. On the fourth push she pulled out something small and swallowed.
"She found that without seeing," Kayal whispered.
"The tip of her beak can feel," said Shanthi. "She feels the worm move in the mud."

Further out, forty or fifty birds with the same long beaks were feeding in a line. The godwit fed for a few minutes more. Then she opened her wings, showed the white bar that Kayal had seen, and flew low over the water to join them.
Appa was still holding the jar lid of rice. He looked at it. Then he tipped it out on the bund for the sparrows.
story.epiphany: Kayal read the bird's food from her body. A long, thin beak is weak at the tip, so it is made for reaching and not for cracking. Long legs and wide, bare toes are for soft mud. So Kayal knew the bird needed a mudflat, and that no food from the kitchen would do.
ask: Why could the long beak not crack a grain of rice?
Which two things about the feet showed that the bird belonged on mud?
Why would the park or the deep temple tank have been the wrong place to let the bird go?

The girl holding a phone to her ear and pointing at the box, with a pair of craft scissors on the floor beside her.
