games.title: Whose Beak, Whose Feet? The clue cards
games.context: This is a card game about eighteen Indian birds. Each card describes a beak and a pair of feet, and you work out what the bird eats.

setup.art: Eighteen cards in a shuffled pile on a table, clue side up, with a small bowl of dried beans beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards. Shuffle them with the clue side up.

setup.art: A child holding one card and reading the clue aloud to a parent and a friend.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the beak and feet clue. The back stays hidden.

setup.art: A child taking a bean from the bowl while the reader shows the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Say the food and how the bird feeds. A right answer wins a bean.

printables.title: 18 clue cards: a beak and feet on the front, the bird and the food on the back

items.f: Beak: short, thick and cone-shaped. Feet: small, with three toes forward and one back.
items.b: House sparrow. She cracks seeds and grain. The short, thick beak bites hard. The feet perch on wires and twigs.

items.f: Beak: long, thin and curved downward. Feet: tiny perching feet.
items.b: Purple sunbird. He drinks nectar from deep inside flowers, and also takes small insects. The thin beak reaches where a thick beak cannot.

items.f: Beak: sharp and hooked. Feet: strong, with long curved talons.
items.b: Black kite. She eats meat, fish and scraps. The talons grip the food and the hook tears it.

items.f: Beak: long, straight and heavy, like a dagger. Feet: small and weak.
items.b: White-throated kingfisher. She drops from a perch on to fish, frogs, lizards and big insects. The long beak snaps shut fast. She hardly walks, so her feet are small.

items.f: Beak: short, thick and strongly hooked. Feet: two toes forward and two back.
items.b: Rose-ringed parakeet. She cracks seeds and bites fruit. The feet climb, and one foot holds the food like a hand.

items.f: Beak: straight and hard, like a chisel. Feet: two toes forward and two back, with sharp claws.
items.b: Woodpecker, such as the black-rumped flameback. She cuts into bark for ants and grubs. The feet hold her upright on a tree trunk.

items.f: Beak: wide and flat, with edges like a comb. Feet: webbed.
items.b: Spot-billed duck. She strains water plants, seeds and small animals from the water. The webbed feet paddle.

items.f: Beak: thick and bent in the middle, used upside down in water. Legs: very long. Feet: webbed.
items.b: Greater flamingo. She strains tiny shrimps and other small life from shallow salty water. The long legs keep her body dry.

items.f: Beak: straight and as long as a pencil. Legs: long. Feet: long toes with no web.
items.b: Black-tailed godwit. She pushes her beak deep into soft mud for worms and snails. The long toes keep her from sinking.

items.f: Beak: short and hooked, half hidden in face feathers. Feet: feathered legs with sharp talons.
items.b: Barn owl. She catches rats and mice at night, and swallows them whole. The talons kill the prey.

items.f: Beak: short and strong. Feet: big, with thick toes and blunt claws.
items.b: Indian peafowl. They scratch the ground for seeds, insects, lizards and small snakes. The strong toes do the digging.

items.f: Beak: short and pointed. Feet: toes and claws so long that each foot is wider than the body.
items.b: Jacana, such as the bronze-winged jacana. She walks on floating leaves and picks insects and seeds from them. The long toes spread her weight.

items.f: Beak: long, thin and slightly curved. Feet: small. The bird sits on a wire and flies out again and again.
items.b: Green bee-eater. She catches bees, wasps and dragonflies in the air. She beats a bee on the perch to remove the sting.

items.f: Beak: huge, long and curved, yellow and black. Feet: broad perching feet. The bird lives in tall forest.
items.b: Great hornbill. They eat figs and other fruit, and some small animals. The long beak picks fruit from thin twigs. A quick toss of the head sends each fruit down the throat.

items.f: Beak: straight, strong and of middle length. Feet: plain perching feet that also walk well.
items.b: House crow. She eats almost anything: grain, fruit, eggs, insects, scraps and dead animals. A plain beak can do many jobs fairly well.

items.f: Beak: very long and heavy, curved a little at the tip. Legs: very long. The bird wades with the beak held open in the water.
items.b: Painted stork. She feels for fish with her open beak. The beak snaps shut the moment a fish touches the inside.

items.f: Beak: long, with a gap between the two halves even when shut. Legs: long.
items.b: Asian openbill, a stork. She eats large water snails. The beak holds the round, slippery shell while she gets the snail out.

items.f: Beak: large and strongly hooked. Feet: big, flat and weak, with blunt claws.
items.b: Vulture, such as the white-rumped vulture. She eats animals who are already dead. The hook tears the meat. The feet only need to walk, so the claws are blunt.

printables.title: Score sheet
items: Player: ___  Bird named too (1 extra bean each): ___
Playing alone: cards right on the first go: ___ out of 18

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the clue side up. Put about 40 dried beans in a bowl.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the clue aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
The player on the reader's left says what the bird eats and how the bird feeds. The answer must use the beak or the feet as the reason.
The reader turns the card over and reads the back. If the food is right, the player takes one bean.
If the player also named the bird, they take one more bean.
If the food is wrong, the next player may try once for one bean.
The card goes to the bottom of the pile, and the next player becomes the reader.
The game ends when all 18 cards have been read. The player with the most beans wins.
If you play alone, read each clue, say your answer aloud and then turn the card over. Make one pile for right answers and one for wrong. Play the wrong pile again.

flow.do: Cut out the 18 cards. Shuffle them, clue side up. Put a bowl of dried beans on the table.
flow.say: Each card describes the beak and feet of a real Indian bird. You will work out the food from those two clues.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and shuffle them. Keep the clue side up.
flow.context: This is the first step of Whose Beak, Whose Feet. You set up the cards and the beans.

flow.do: Play by the rules until all 18 cards have been read. After each card, ask for the reason before the card is turned over.
flow.say: Tell me the food, and tell me which part of the beak or feet made you think so. Then we turn the card over.
flow.kid: Listen to the clue. Say what the bird eats, and why.
flow.parent: Accept any food that fits the back of the card. For the crow, 'almost anything' is the right answer. If your child is stuck, ask whether the beak is made for a hard bite or a long reach.

check.q: A card says: short hooked beak, and strong feet with long curved talons. What does this bird most likely eat?
check.why: Talons grip and kill prey, and a hook tears meat. If you chose seeds, remember that a seed-cracker's beak is a thick cone with no hook.

flow.context: In this step of Whose Beak, Whose Feet you play through all 18 cards.

flow.do: Lay out the vulture card and the kite card side by side. Ask what is the same and what is different. Then do the same with the godwit and the sparrow.
flow.say: The vulture and the kite both have hooked beaks. Their feet are very different. What does that tell you about how each one gets meat?
flow.kid: Put the kite and the vulture together. What differs? Say why.

ask.q: Why does a vulture not need talons?
good: The animal is already dead, so there is nothing to catch.
She only walks and stands on the food.

flow.think: Which of the 18 birds on the cards would find food most easily in your street?
flow.context: This is the last step of Whose Beak, Whose Feet. You compare two pairs of birds.

games.title: Bird, Old Dinosaur or Both? The feature cards
games.context: This is a sorting game about what birds share with the dinosaurs of long ago. Each card names one feature, and you decide who had it.

setup.art: Three paper labels in a row on the floor: Only birds alive today, Only the old dinosaurs, and Both.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the three labels in a row.

setup.art: A child reading a card that says Has a wishbone and holding it over the three labels.
setup.caption: 2. Read a feature card. Put it under one label.

setup.art: The same child turning over the cards under the Both label and looking surprised at how many there are.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the cards over to check. Count the cards under Both.

printables.title: 16 feature cards: a feature on the front, the answer and the evidence on the back

items.f: Has feathers
items.b: Both. Sinosauropteryx, found in China in 1996, had short feathers and could not fly.

items.f: Lays eggs with hard shells
items.b: Both. Fossil nests of theropod eggs have been found in Mongolia and China.

items.f: Sits on the eggs in a nest
items.b: Both. Fossils of Citipati were found sitting on nests with the arms spread over the eggs.

items.f: Has a wishbone
items.b: Both. Velociraptor and Tyrannosaurus had wishbones.

items.f: Has hollow bones
items.b: Both. Theropod bones were hollow, as a hen's leg bones are.

items.f: Walks on two legs, on the toes
items.b: Both. Theropod footprints show the toes only. The heel stayed off the ground.

items.f: Has three main toes pointing forward
items.b: Both. Theropod footprints in rock look like very large bird footprints.

items.f: Has scaly skin on the feet
items.b: Both. Skin prints of dinosaurs show scales, and a hen's feet are scaly.

items.f: Has teeth in the jaws
items.b: Only the old dinosaurs. No bird alive today has teeth. Some early birds did.

items.f: Has a long bony tail
items.b: Only the old dinosaurs. A bird's tail bones are few and joined into one short stump.

items.f: Has a beak with no teeth
items.b: Both. Citipati and their relatives had beaks with no teeth, long before today's birds.

items.f: Sings with a voice box at the bottom of the windpipe
items.b: Only birds, as far as we know. The oldest fossil of this voice box is from a bird of about 67 million years ago.

items.f: Sleeps with the head tucked under one arm or wing
items.b: Both. A small dinosaur named Mei long was found curled up in this pose.

items.f: Swallows small stones that help to grind food
items.b: Both. Polished stones have been found inside the fossils of some small feathered dinosaurs.

items.f: Can weigh more than an elephant
items.b: Only the old dinosaurs. The heaviest bird alive, the ostrich, weighs about as much as two grown people.

items.f: Is alive today
items.b: Only birds. Every other dinosaur died out about 66 million years ago.

rules: Lay the three labels in a row on the floor or a table.
Shuffle the 16 feature cards and hold them with the feature side up.
Read the top card. Decide who has this feature: only birds alive today, only the old dinosaurs, or both.
Put the card under the label you chose. Do not turn it over yet.
With two or more players, take turns. The other players may say 'I disagree' and give a reason.
When all 16 cards are placed, turn them over one at a time and read the backs.
Each player scores one point for every card they placed correctly. If you play alone, count how many of the 16 you placed correctly.
Last, count the cards that belong under Both.

flow.do: Lay out the three labels. Shuffle the 16 cards. Ask your child to guess how many cards will end up under Both.
flow.say: Here are 16 features. Some belong only to birds. Some belong only to the dinosaurs of long ago. Some belong to both. How many of the 16 do you think both will share? Why?
flow.kid: Guess how many of the 16 cards go under Both.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bird, Old Dinosaur or Both. You set up and make a guess.

flow.do: Play by the rules. Let your child place every card before any card is turned over.
flow.say: Read each feature and choose a label. Give me one reason each time. We check them all at the end.
flow.kid: Read each card. Put it under a label. Say why.
flow.parent: Most children put feathers, wishbones and sitting on eggs under 'Only birds'. Let those stand until the cards are turned over.
flow.context: In this step of Bird, Old Dinosaur or Both you sort all 16 feature cards.

flow.do: Turn the cards over and read the backs. Count the cards under each label. Ask your child what surprised them.
flow.say: Eleven of the 16 features belong to both. Which one surprised you most? What does it tell you about where birds came from?
flow.kid: Turn the cards over. Count the Both pile. Which card surprised you?

check.q: Which of these features did small meat-eating dinosaurs share with birds?
check.why: Fossils show feathers and wishbones on small theropods. If you chose another answer, look again at the cards under 'Only birds alive today'.

flow.context: This is the last step of Bird, Old Dinosaur or Both. You check the cards and count how many features are shared.

experiments.title: The Beak Lever Test: where does a beak bite hardest?
experiments.question: Scissors have two blades joined at a hinge, like the two halves of a beak. Do the blades cut a thicker stack of paper near the hinge, in the middle or at the tips? How wide do they open at each place?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Where will the scissors cut the thickest stack of newspaper: near the hinge, in the middle or at the tips? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same scissors and the same newspaper for every cut. The same person makes every cut, with one hand and one squeeze. Use the same three places on the blades each time, and mark them first. Check each result twice. Only one thing changes: the place on the blades where the paper sits.
results_table: Thickest stack cut in one squeeze (layers)

materials.item: ordinary paper scissors, with blades about 8 to 10 centimetres long (not nail scissors and not sharp kitchen scissors)
full sheets of old newspaper
a ruler
a sketch pen, or three small bits of sticking tape, to mark the blades
a notebook page and a pencil for the results

experiments.safety: A grown-up stays beside the child for every cut. Keep the fingers that hold the paper well away from the blades. If a stack does not cut with one firm squeeze, stop and record that. Do not force the scissors.
experiments.record: Make a table with three rows: near the hinge, middle and tips. In each row write the thickest stack the scissors cut in one squeeze, and the gap between the open blades.
experiments.context: In this experiment a pair of scissors is your model of a beak. You find where along the blades the cut is strongest, and where the blades open widest.

setup.art: A pair of open scissors lying on a table with three pen marks on one blade: one 2 centimetres from the screw, one in the middle and one near the tip.
setup.caption: 1. Mark three places on one blade: near the hinge, the middle and the tips.

setup.art: Five folded wads of newspaper in a row, from thin to thick, labelled 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32.
setup.caption: 2. Fold newspaper into five stacks: 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 layers.

setup.art: A child cutting into a folded newspaper stack with only the tips of the scissors, while a grown-up watches.
setup.caption: 3. Cut each stack with the tips only. Use one hand and one squeeze.

setup.art: The same child cutting a thick stack with the part of the blades closest to the screw.
setup.caption: 4. Do the same in the middle, and then near the hinge.

setup.art: Open scissors on a table with a ruler held across the blades near the screw, and a dotted line showing a second measurement at the tips.
setup.caption: 5. Open the scissors wide. Measure the gap near the hinge and at the tips.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results. Your numbers will differ.
rows: Near the hinge, 2 cm from the screw

flow.do: Show your child the scissors. Open and shut them slowly. Point to the screw, which is the hinge. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: These scissors are our model beak. The screw is the hinge, like the joint at the back of a bird's mouth. Where will the blades cut the thickest stack: near the hinge, in the middle or at the tips? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Open and shut the scissors. Look at the hinge, the middle and the tips.

ask.q: Why do you think that place will cut best?
good: The tips are sharp and pointed.
Near the hinge feels stronger when I cut card.
The middle is where I usually cut.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children choose the tips because they look sharp.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Beak Lever Test. You guess where the scissors cut hardest, before you test.

flow.do: Mark one blade at 2 centimetres from the screw, in the middle, and 1 centimetre from the tip. Tear the newspaper into five pieces, each about the size of a notebook page. Fold the first piece once and the second twice. Fold the third 3 times, the fourth 4 times and the fifth 5 times.
flow.say: Every fold doubles the layers. One fold makes 2 layers. Two folds make 4. How many layers will five folds make?
flow.kid: Mark the blade in three places. Fold five stacks: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 layers.
flow.parent: Five folds make 32 layers. Press each fold flat with a thumbnail. Write the number of layers on each stack.
flow.context: In this step of the Beak Lever Test you mark the scissors and fold five stacks of newspaper.

flow.do: Start with the tips. Slide the stack of 2 layers between the tips only. Squeeze once with one hand. Then try 4, 8, 16 and 32 layers. Write down the thickest stack that was cut right through. Check that stack once more. Then do the same in the middle, and then near the hinge.
flow.say: Put the paper only at the mark we are testing. Squeeze once, with one hand, as hard as is comfortable. A cut counts only if every layer is cut through.
flow.kid: Cut with the tips first. Then the middle. Then near the hinge.

check.q: In the Beak Lever Test, why do you use the same hand and one squeeze for every cut?
options: So only the place on the blades changes
So the paper does not tear
check.why: If you squeezed harder at one place, you could not tell what made the difference. If you chose another answer, remember that a fair test changes one thing only.

flow.parent: At the tips, a thick stack often slides forward out of the blades without being cut. That is a real result, so record it. Near the hinge most scissors cut 16 layers, and some cut 32.
flow.context: In this step of the Beak Lever Test you find the thickest stack the scissors can cut at each place.

flow.do: Open the scissors as wide as they go and lay them on the table. Measure the gap between the two blades at the mark near the hinge. Then measure the gap at the tips. Write both numbers in the table.
flow.say: Now we measure how far the blades open. Look at the gap near the hinge and the gap at the tips.
flow.kid: Open the scissors wide. Measure the gap at the hinge and the tips.

ask.q: Which part of the blades moves fastest when the scissors snap shut?
good: The tips, because they travel farthest in the same time.

flow.context: In this step of the Beak Lever Test you measure how wide the blades open at two places.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. Wait for all three. Then read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your table. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Look at your table. Tell your grown-up what you found.

ask.q: Where was the cut strongest, and where did the blades open widest?
good: Strongest near the hinge.
Widest at the tips.
The strong place and the wide place are at opposite ends.

flow.parent: The explanation: each blade is a lever, which is a stiff bar that turns about a hinge. Your hand's squeeze is passed along the blade. Close to the hinge it arrives as a strong push over a short distance. Far from the hinge it arrives as a weak push over a long distance. So the blades cut hardest near the hinge, and open widest and move fastest at the tips.
flow.context: In this step of the Beak Lever Test you explain your results in your own words.

flow.do: Ask your child to use the result on two birds: a sparrow with a beak about 1 centimetre long, and a godwit with a beak about 10 centimetres long.
flow.say: A sparrow's whole beak is as short as the part of the scissors near the hinge. A godwit's beak is as long as the whole blade. Which bird can crack a hard seed? What can the other bird do that this one cannot?
flow.kid: Match each bird to a part of the scissors.

check.q: A bird has a very long, thin beak. What is this beak best at?
check.why: The tip of a long beak is far from the hinge, so the bite there is weak. But the tip reaches far and moves fast. If you chose cracking seeds, look at your table: the tips cut the thinnest stack.

flow.think: Why does a finch move a very hard seed to the back of her beak before she bites?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Beak Lever Test. You use your result to compare a short beak and a long beak.

experiments.title: The Frozen Mud Test: can a probing beak find food in frozen ground?
experiments.question: Ten beans are hidden in a bowl of soft mud, and ten in a bowl of frozen mud. How many can tweezers find in 30 seconds in each bowl? How long must frozen mud stand in the room before the tweezers can find food again?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many of the ten beans will you find in the soft mud in 30 seconds? How many in the frozen mud? How many after the frozen bowl has stood in the room for 20 minutes? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two bowls of the same size, with the same amount of mud and ten beans in each. A grown-up hides the beans at the same depth in both. The same person searches each time, with the same tweezers, one hand and 30 seconds on a timer. Only one thing changes: whether the mud is soft or frozen.

materials.item: steel bowls of the same size, about 10 centimetres wide
wet soil from a plant pot, about 2 cups (or wet sand, or used tea leaves saved for two days)
dried rajma beans, chana or groundnuts, to be the hidden food
tweezers (or a U-shaped hairpin, or two thin sticks held together like tongs)
a steel plate to cover one bowl in the freezer
a phone timer, a notebook page and a pencil

experiments.safety: Wash your hands with soap after touching the soil. Cover the bowl before it goes into the freezer, and keep it away from food.

schedule.what: Make two bowls of mud with ten hidden beans each. Put one bowl in the freezer overnight.
Search both bowls for 30 seconds each. Search the frozen bowl again after 20 and 40 minutes in the room.

experiments.record: Make a table with four rows: soft mud, frozen mud, frozen mud after 20 minutes in the room, and frozen mud after 40 minutes. Write the number of beans found in 30 seconds in each row.
experiments.context: In this experiment tweezers are the beak of a godwit, a bird who feeds by pushing her beak into mud. You test whether that beak can still find food when the mud freezes.

setup.art: Two steel bowls of dark wet mud on a kitchen counter, with a small heap of rajma beans and a pair of tweezers beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Fill two bowls with wet mud, about 3 centimetres deep.

setup.art: A grown-up pushing a bean into the mud with one finger while a child looks away.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up hides ten beans in each bowl, about 2 centimetres deep.

setup.art: One bowl covered with a steel plate on a freezer shelf, and the other bowl on the counter.
setup.caption: 3. Cover one bowl and freeze it overnight. Keep the other in the room.

setup.art: A child pushing tweezers into the soft mud and lifting out a bean, with a phone timer showing 30 seconds.
setup.caption: 4. Search each bowl with tweezers for 30 seconds. Count the beans.

setup.art: The frozen bowl standing on the counter with a wet shine on top of the mud and a clock behind it.
setup.caption: 5. Search the frozen bowl again after 20 minutes and after 40 minutes.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results. Your numbers will differ.
rows: Frozen mud, straight from the freezer
Frozen mud after 20 minutes in the room
Frozen mud after 40 minutes in the room

flow.do: Show your child the tweezers and the soil. Ask for the three guesses and the reasons. Write them down.
flow.say: A godwit feeds by pushing her long beak into soft mud. The tweezers are her beak. I will hide ten beans in soft mud and ten in mud that I freeze. How many will you find in each in 30 seconds? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The tweezers are a godwit's beak. Guess how many beans you will find. Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Frozen Mud Test. You guess how many hidden beans a beak can find in soft mud and in frozen mud.

flow.do: Day 1. Mix the soil with water until it is thick, shiny mud. Fill both bowls to about 3 centimetres deep. Send your child out. Push ten beans into each bowl, about 2 centimetres down, and smooth the top. Cover one bowl with a plate and put it in the freezer. Leave the other bowl in the room, covered with a damp cloth.
flow.say: Please wait outside for two minutes. I am hiding ten beans in each bowl. One bowl goes into the freezer until tomorrow.
flow.kid: Help to mix the mud. Then wait outside while the beans are hidden.
flow.parent: If you have no soil, wet sand or a thick paste of used tea leaves works. The mud must be wet enough to shine, or it will not freeze hard.
flow.wait: Leave the bowl in the freezer overnight, or for at least 4 hours
flow.context: In this step of the Frozen Mud Test a grown-up hides ten beans in each bowl and freezes one bowl.

flow.do: Day 2. Take the frozen bowl out. Give your child the tweezers and the soft bowl first. Time 30 seconds. Count the beans found. Then time 30 seconds on the frozen bowl. Write both numbers down.
flow.say: Use one hand and only the tweezers. You have 30 seconds for each bowl. Push the tips in, feel for a bean and lift the bean out.
flow.kid: Search the soft bowl for 30 seconds. Then search the frozen bowl.

check.q: In the Frozen Mud Test, are the ten beans still inside the frozen bowl?
options: Yes, but the tweezers cannot reach them
No, they moved to the other bowl
check.why: Freezing did not remove the food. It made the mud too hard for a thin beak to enter. If you chose another answer, wait until the mud thaws and count the beans.

flow.context: In this step of the Frozen Mud Test you search the soft mud and the frozen mud with tweezers.

flow.do: Leave the frozen bowl on the counter. Search it again for 30 seconds when 20 minutes have passed, and again when 40 minutes have passed. Write down each count.
flow.say: The bowl is warming up. Feel the top with the tweezers. Has anything changed? You have 30 seconds again.
flow.kid: Wait 20 minutes. Search again. Then wait 20 more and search again.
flow.parent: Use the waits for the term cards or a game. On a hot day the top thaws faster, so the counts will be higher.
flow.context: In this step of the Frozen Mud Test you search the frozen bowl again as it thaws in the room.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. Wait for all three. Then read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your four counts. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Then tell me what a godwit must do when the ground where she lives freezes.
flow.kid: Look at your table. Tell your grown-up what you found.

ask.q: The food was in the frozen bowl all the time. Why did the beak go hungry?
good: The mud was too hard to push into.
A thin beak cannot break ice.

ask.q: Would a sparrow, who picks seeds off the top of the ground, have the same problem?
good: Less so, unless snow covers the seeds.
She does not need to push into the ground.

flow.parent: The explanation: godwits nest in Central Asia and Siberia, where the summer mud is soft and full of worms. In winter that ground freezes for months. The worms are still there, and a thin beak cannot reach them. So the godwits fly to India, where the mud stays soft, and fly back in spring. Tip the mud back into the plant pot when you finish.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Frozen Mud Test. You explain your results and link them to migration.

activities.title: Beak and Feet Watch: ten minutes with one bird

materials.item: a notebook page and a pencil
a window or a balcony (or a phone video of a crow or a pigeon walking and feeding, if no bird comes)

schedule.what: Watch one bird, draw the beak and one foot, and write down what the bird does with each.

activities.record: The number of toes pointing forward and back. A list of everything you saw the bird do with the beak and with the feet.
activities.context: In this activity you find out what a bird's beak and feet are for. You watch one bird closely for a few minutes.

setup.art: A child at a window with a notebook, looking at a crow on the balcony rail.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one bird that you can see clearly. A crow or a pigeon is fine.

setup.art: A notebook page with a large drawing of a crow's beak and a foot showing three toes forward and one back.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the beak and one foot. Count the toes.

setup.art: The same page with a short list: picks up rice, wipes beak on rail, scratches head with foot.
setup.caption: 3. List what the beak does and what the feet do.

flow.do: Choose one bird at the window. If no bird comes within two minutes, play a phone video of a crow or a pigeon feeding. Ask your child to look at the beak and guess the food.
flow.say: Look only at the beak. Is it long or short, thick or thin, straight or hooked? What do you think this bird eats? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the beak. What do you think this bird eats? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Beak and Feet Watch. You pick a bird and guess the food from the beak.

flow.do: Watch for five minutes. Your child looks at the beak and one foot, and counts the toes pointing forward and back. They list everything the bird does with the beak and with the feet.
flow.say: Look at the beak and one foot. How many toes point forward, and how many point back? Write down each thing the beak does. Write down whether the bird walks or hops.
flow.kid: Count the toes. List what the beak and the feet do.
flow.parent: A crow or a pigeon has three toes forward and one back. A pigeon and a crow walk, and a sparrow hops. A beak is often used to clean feathers and to scratch, as well as to eat.
flow.context: In this step of Beak and Feet Watch you draw the beak and a foot. You also list what the bird does with them.

flow.do: Ask your child to read out the list. Ask which jobs of the beak had nothing to do with eating.
flow.say: Read me your list out loud. Then we look for beak jobs that were not eating.
flow.kid: Read your list out loud.

ask.q: What did the beak do besides eating?
good: Cleaned the feathers.
Carried a twig.
Pecked at another bird.
Wiped the beak clean on the rail.

flow.think: You have hands and teeth. Which jobs of your hands and teeth does a bird do with her beak?
flow.context: This is the last step of Beak and Feet Watch. You read out what the beak and feet did.

activities.title: The Sleeping Grip: how tendons close a hand or a foot

materials.item: a table to rest your elbow on
a pencil
a helper

schedule.what: Bend your wrist back and forward, and watch what your fingers do without being told.

activities.record: What your fingers did with the wrist bent back, and what they did with the wrist bent forward. Say it, write it, or draw your hand each time.
activities.context: In this activity you find out how bending one joint can close the fingers, using your own hand. It shows one way a bird's toes can hold a branch while the bird sleeps.

setup.art: A child's elbow resting on a table with the hand hanging limp, and a helper gently pressing the back of the hand so that the wrist bends back.
setup.caption: 1. Let your hand hang loose. A helper bends your wrist back. Watch your fingers.

setup.art: The same hand with the wrist bent forward and the fingers hanging open.
setup.caption: 2. The helper bends your wrist forward. Watch your fingers again.

setup.art: A child holding a pencil loosely in a bent-forward hand while a helper pulls the pencil away with two fingers.
setup.caption: 3. Hold a pencil loosely. The helper pulls it, with your wrist forward and then back.

flow.do: Ask your child the question about the sleeping myna. Write down the guess.
flow.say: A myna sleeps for about ten hours on a thin branch. She does not fall off. How do you think her toes stay closed while she sleeps?
flow.kid: A myna sleeps on a branch all night. Why does she not fall?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Sleeping Grip. You guess how a sleeping bird stays on a branch.

flow.do: Your child rests an elbow on the table and lets the hand hang loose. Gently bend their wrist back as far as is comfortable. Then gently bend it forward. Do it three times. Your child watches the fingers.
flow.say: Keep your hand as loose as a wet cloth. Do not move your fingers yourself. I will bend your wrist back, and then forward. Tell me what your fingers do.
flow.kid: Keep your hand loose. Watch your fingers as your wrist bends.
flow.parent: With the wrist bent back, the loose fingers curl. With the wrist bent forward, they open. Bend gently and stop if it is uncomfortable.
flow.context: In this step of The Sleeping Grip a helper bends your wrist, and you watch your loose fingers.

flow.do: Your child holds a pencil loosely across the fingers, with the wrist bent far forward. Pull the pencil gently. Then your child bends the wrist back and holds the pencil in the same loose way. Pull again.
flow.say: Hold the pencil loosely, with your wrist bent forward. I will pull it gently. Now bend your wrist back and hold it loosely again. Which time was the pencil harder to pull out?
flow.kid: Hold a pencil loosely. Bend your wrist forward, then back.
flow.context: In this step of The Sleeping Grip you test your grip on a pencil with the wrist bent two ways.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they saw and why they think it happened. Then read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what your fingers did when your wrist bent back, and why you think it happened. Then find the cords on the inside of your wrist. Wiggle your fingers and feel the cords move.
flow.kid: Say what your fingers did. Say why. Then feel the cords in your wrist.

ask.q: You did not move your fingers. What pulled them closed?
good: Something inside my arm pulled them.
The cords in my wrist got tight.

flow.parent: The explanation: the muscles that close your fingers are in your forearm. Tough cords called tendons join them to your finger bones, and cross the wrist. Bending the wrist back pulls those tendons tight, so the fingers curl. A bird's toe tendons run down the back of the leg in a similar way. They also have tiny bumps that catch on ridges, which helps to keep the toes shut. Scientists still argue about how much a sleeping bird relies on this.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Sleeping Grip. You explain what closed your fingers and compare your hand with a bird's foot.

activities.title: Find the Dinosaur in a Bird

materials.item: a bird at the window, or a phone video of a hen or a pigeon walking
a notebook page and a pencil
if your family cooks chicken, the cleaned wishbone and one leg bone from a cooked chicken. You can do the activity without them.

schedule.what: Check eight features on a bird, and guess which of them small meat-eating dinosaurs had.

activities.record: A table with eight rows, one for each feature, and two columns: 'Bird' and 'Small meat-eating dinosaurs: my guess'. Put a tick or a cross in each box.
activities.context: In this activity you check a bird for eight features. Then you guess which of them were also found on small meat-eating dinosaurs such as Velociraptor.

setup.art: A notebook table with eight rows labelled feathers, scaly feet, claws, three front toes, walks on toes, lays hard eggs, sits on eggs, wishbone, and two empty columns.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table with eight features and two columns.

setup.art: A pigeon on a window ledge seen from the side, with the foot, the scaly leg and the raised ankle clearly shown.
setup.caption: 2. Check each feature on a real bird or a video.

setup.art: A child standing on tiptoe beside a drawing of a hen's leg, with arrows joining the child's raised heel to the hen's backward-pointing joint.
setup.caption: 3. Stand on your toes. Your raised heel matches the bird's backward joint.

setup.art: The notebook table with ticks in the Bird column and a child's pencil hovering over the second column.
setup.caption: 4. Guess which features the small dinosaurs had. Then check.

flow.do: Make the table with eight rows. The first four rows are feathers, scaly feet, claws on the toes, and three main toes pointing forward. The last four are walks on the toes, lays eggs with hard shells, sits on the eggs, and a wishbone.
flow.say: We are going to check a bird for eight features. Then you will guess which of the eight a small meat-eating dinosaur had. Make the table first.
flow.kid: Make a table with eight rows. Write one feature in each row.
flow.context: This is the first step of Find the Dinosaur in a Bird. You draw a table of eight features.

flow.do: Watch a bird at the window, or a video of a hen or pigeon walking. Tick each feature you can see. Then your child stands on tiptoe and feels their own raised heel and ankle.
flow.say: Look at the leg. The joint that seems to bend backward is not a knee. Stand on your toes. Your heel is up in the air now, just as hers is.
flow.kid: Tick what you see on the bird. Then stand on your toes. Feel your heel.
flow.parent: A bird walks on the toes all the time. The backward-pointing joint is the ankle, and the real knee is hidden in the feathers. You cannot see eggs or a wishbone at the window, so tick those from what you know. If you have a chicken wishbone, show it now.

check.q: A hen's leg has a joint that points backward. Which joint is it?
check.why: A bird stands on the toes, so the ankle is lifted high off the ground. If you chose the knee, stand on tiptoe: your knee still points forward and your heel points back.

flow.context: In this step of Find the Dinosaur in a Bird you check the features on a real bird. You also compare the bird's leg with your own.

flow.do: Ask your child to fill in the second column with guesses. Ask for a reason for at least two of them.
flow.say: Now think of a small meat-eating dinosaur, such as Velociraptor. Which of these eight features do you think they had? Put a tick or a cross for each. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which features a small dinosaur had. Tick or cross each one.
flow.context: In this step of Find the Dinosaur in a Bird you guess which bird features small meat-eating dinosaurs had.

flow.do: Tell your child the answer after they have guessed. Fossils show all eight features on small meat-eating dinosaurs. Then ask what a hen does not have that those dinosaurs had.
flow.say: Fossils show every one of the eight on small meat-eating dinosaurs. Look at your guesses. Which ones were right?
flow.kid: All eight are found in fossils. What does that tell you about birds?

ask.q: What did Velociraptor have that a hen does not?
good: Teeth.
A long bony tail.
Hands with three clawed fingers.

flow.parent: The evidence: Sinosauropteryx had short feathers. Velociraptor's arm bone has the small knobs where long feathers were fixed, and a Velociraptor wishbone was described in 1997. Citipati was found sitting on a nest of hard-shelled eggs. Footprints show three front toes and no heel mark.
flow.think: If a hen is a dinosaur, when did the last dinosaur die?
flow.context: This is the last step of Find the Dinosaur in a Bird. You compare your guesses with what fossils show.

activities.title: Where Would You Nest? Four places, four problems

materials.item: a notebook page and a pencil
four slips of paper
dry grass, twigs, leaves or scrap paper

schedule.what: Design a nest for each of four places, and compare your designs with what real birds do.

activities.record: Four small nests, one for each place (or drawings, if you prefer). Beside each, write the main danger there and how your nest deals with it.
activities.context: In this activity you find out why birds nest in such different places. For each of four places you work out the danger, then make a nest that deals with it.

setup.art: Four paper slips on a table reading: open stony ground, a tall tree where snakes climb, under a concrete bridge, a big tree with an old hole.
setup.caption: 1. Write the four places on four slips.

setup.art: A child drawing a hanging nest at the tip of a thin branch over water.
setup.caption: 2. For each place, name the danger and make a nest.

setup.art: The child's four drawings beside four small drawings of a lapwing scrape, a weaver nest, a swallow mud nest and a sealed hornbill hole.
setup.caption: 3. Compare your nests with the real ones.

flow.do: Write the four places on four slips. The first two are open stony ground with no plants, and a tall tree where snakes climb. The last two are the underside of a concrete bridge, and a big tree with an old hole.
flow.say: A nest has two jobs. It keeps the eggs warm, and it keeps hunters away from eggs and chicks. Here are four places. What is the biggest danger to an egg in each one?
flow.kid: Read the four slips. Think about the danger to an egg in each place.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Would You Nest. You look at four places and name the danger in each.

flow.do: Your child makes a small nest on each slip from grass, twigs, leaves or scraps, or just describes it. They say how it deals with the danger. Do not show the real answers yet.
flow.say: Make a nest on each slip. You have only a beak and two feet. Use grass, twigs, leaves or scraps. Tell me how each nest keeps the eggs safe.
flow.kid: Make a nest on each slip. Say how it keeps the eggs safe.
flow.parent: Any design with a reason is good. Ask how the bird would carry and fix each material with only a beak.
flow.context: In this step of Where Would You Nest you design a nest for each of the four places.

flow.do: Read out what real birds do, from the note below. Ask your child which real nest is closest to their own design, and which surprised them.
flow.say: Now hear what four real birds do in these four places. Which one is closest to your design? Which one would you never have thought of?
flow.kid: Hear what real birds do. Which nest is like yours?
flow.parent: Open ground: a red-wattled lapwing builds almost nothing. The eggs are speckled like the stones, and the parents call loudly and lead hunters away. A tree with snakes: a baya weaver hangs a woven nest from the thin tip of a branch. The long entrance tube points down. Under a bridge: a red-rumped swallow sticks a nest of mud pellets to the concrete. A tree hole: a great hornbill mother seals herself inside and leaves only a narrow slit.
flow.think: Which of the four nests costs the parents the most work? Which costs the least?
flow.context: This is the last step of Where Would You Nest. You compare your designs with the nests of four real birds.

projects.title: From Crocodile to Sparrow: a family tree on the wall

materials.item: sheets of plain paper or old calendar pages, cut into cards about the size of your hand
sketch pens or colour pencils
wool or string, about 3 metres
sticking tape or reusable putty for the wall

schedule.what: Arrange the cards as a branching tree on the wall and add the feature marks.
Show the tree to your family and ask them three questions.

projects.record: A tree of eight cards on a wall or a door, with six feature marks on the main line. A note of what your family guessed and what surprised them.
projects.context: In this three-day project you build a family tree on a wall. You will find out which animals are the sparrow's closest relatives. It shows how a crocodile, five dinosaurs of long ago, a hen and a sparrow are related.

setup.art: Eight hand-sized cards on a table with child's drawings of a mugger crocodile, a long-necked dinosaur, Rajasaurus, Tyrannosaurus, Velociraptor, Archaeopteryx, a hen and a sparrow.
setup.caption: 1. Make eight cards, one animal on each.

setup.art: A length of wool taped up a wall as a main line, with the eight cards on short side branches from bottom to top.
setup.caption: 2. Tape a main line of wool to the wall. Add each card on a side branch.

setup.art: Six small paper marks stuck on the main line between the branches, labelled with features such as wishbone, feathers and wings.
setup.caption: 3. Mark on the line where each new feature appears.

flow.do: Day 1. Your child makes eight cards: a mugger crocodile, Barapasaurus, Rajasaurus, Tyrannosaurus, Velociraptor, Archaeopteryx, a hen and a sparrow. On each card they write the name and when the animal lived. They can draw the animal, or stick on a picture, or leave the name alone.
flow.say: Make one card for each animal. Barapasaurus was a long-necked plant-eater found in Telangana. Rajasaurus was a meat-eater found in Gujarat. Which of these eight do you think is the sparrow's closest relative? Why?
flow.kid: Make eight animal cards. Write each name. Guess the sparrow's closest relative.
flow.parent: When each lived: the crocodile, the hen and the sparrow are alive today. Barapasaurus lived about 185 million years ago. Rajasaurus and Tyrannosaurus lived about 67 million years ago. Velociraptor lived about 75 million years ago, and Archaeopteryx about 150 million years ago. Draw Velociraptor with feathers.
flow.context: This is day 1 of From Crocodile to Sparrow. You draw eight animal cards.

flow.do: Day 2. Tape the wool up the wall as one main line. Add the cards on short side branches, from the bottom: crocodile, Barapasaurus, Rajasaurus, Tyrannosaurus, Velociraptor, Archaeopteryx. Put the hen and the sparrow together at the top. Then stick six feature marks on the main line, using the note below.
flow.say: The main line leads to the birds. Each side branch is a relative who split off. A relative higher up is a closer cousin of the sparrow. Now we mark where each new feature first appears on the line.
flow.kid: Tape the line to the wall. Add the cards in order. Stick on the feature marks.
flow.wait: Do this the day after you draw the cards
flow.parent: The six marks, from the bottom. Below Barapasaurus: 'dinosaurs begin: legs straight under the body'. Below Rajasaurus: 'walks on two legs, hollow bones, three main toes, wishbone'. Below Tyrannosaurus: 'simple feathers'. Below Velociraptor: 'long feathers on the arms'. Below Archaeopteryx: 'wings that can fly'. Below the hen and sparrow: 'beak with no teeth, short tail'.
flow.context: This is day 2 of From Crocodile to Sparrow. You arrange the eight cards as a tree and add six feature marks.

flow.do: Day 3. Your child shows the tree to the family and asks three questions. Which animal on the tree is a hen's closest cousin? Which animals on the tree are dinosaurs? Is a crocodile a closer relative of a lizard or of a sparrow? Your child writes down the guesses and then explains the tree.
flow.say: You are the guide today. Ask your three questions before you explain anything. Write down what each person guesses. Then show them the answers on the tree.
flow.kid: Show your tree. Ask your three questions. Then explain the answers.
flow.wait: Do this the day after you build the tree
flow.parent: The answers: the sparrow is the hen's closest cousin on the tree, and Archaeopteryx is the next. Every card except the crocodile is a dinosaur, including the hen and the sparrow. A crocodile is a closer relative of a sparrow than of a lizard. Crocodiles and dinosaurs share a more recent ancestor than the one that they share with lizards.
flow.think: Where would you put yourself on a bigger tree that had room for every animal?
flow.context: This is day 3 of From Crocodile to Sparrow. You show the family tree to your family and ask them three questions.

challenges.title: Stick a Nest to a Wall: build with pellets like a swallow
challenges.problem: A red-rumped swallow has no hands and no glue. She carries wet mud in her beak, one small pellet at a time. She sticks about a thousand pellets to the underside of a bridge. Your problem is like hers. Build a nest cup on an upright piece of cardboard, using only small pellets. When it is dry, it must hold three marbles without breaking off.
constraints: Use only pellets no bigger than a chana. Do not press on one big lump.
The cardboard stands upright while you build.
The cup must stick out at least 4 centimetres from the cardboard.
After drying for one day, it must hold three marbles or three large chana for one minute.
materials: a piece of stiff cardboard about the size of a notebook, from an old box
half a cup of sticky wet soil from a plant pot (or a stiff dough of half a cup of old atta and water)
a little dry grass, coconut fibre, or cotton thread cut into short bits
three marbles or three large chana
something to lean the cardboard against, such as a wall or a pile of books
general: Start with a curved line of pellets on the cardboard, shaped like a smile. Build upward and outward from that line.
Wet each pellet a little before pressing it on, so that it sticks to the row below.
Build a few rows, let them dry for some hours, and then add more.
creative: Mix short bits of dry grass or coconut fibre into the pellets. Then cracks do not run through the wall.
Make the wall thick where it joins the cardboard and thin at the rim.
Roughen the cardboard with a fork first, so that the first row has something to hold.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own. Change one thing: the mix, the shape, or how long you wait between rows. Tell your grown-up your plan (or draw it), build it, and test it with the three marbles after one day. Write down what held and what broke.
challenges.context: In this challenge you build a nest cup on an upright cardboard wall using only small pellets. You will find out how a swallow can stick mud to an upright wall without glue.

setup.art: A piece of cardboard leaning upright against a wall, with a bowl of wet soil, a bowl of water and a small heap of rolled pellets beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the cardboard upright. Roll pellets no bigger than a chana.

setup.art: A child pressing a pellet on to a curved row of pellets stuck to the cardboard.
setup.caption: 2. Stick the pellets on one by one, in rows, to build a cup.

setup.art: A dry half-cup of pellets sticking out from the cardboard with three marbles resting inside it.
setup.caption: 3. Let it dry for a day. Test it with three marbles.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Stand the cardboard upright. Ask your child what will make the wet pellets fall off, and how to stop that.
flow.say: The wall is upright, and the pellets are wet and heavy. What could make the nest fall off before it dries? List every idea you have for stopping that.
flow.kid: Read the problem. Think of ideas to stop the pellets falling off.

ask.q: What makes a wet nest fall off an upright wall?
good: Its own weight.
Too much water, so the pellets slide.
Building too far out before the bottom is dry.

flow.context: This is the first step of Stick a Nest to a Wall. You read the problem and think about what could go wrong.

flow.do: Your child rolls pellets and builds the cup, row by row. If the wall starts to sag, they stop and let it dry before adding more.
flow.say: Roll each pellet between your fingers and press it on gently. Build the bottom rows first. If the wall sags, stop and let it dry for a while.
flow.kid: Roll small pellets. Press them on in rows. Stop if the wall sags.
flow.parent: Soil from a pot works only if it is sticky when wet. If it crumbles, use stiff atta dough made with old flour. A cup of about 60 to 80 pellets is enough. Wash hands with soap afterwards.
flow.context: In this step of Stick a Nest to a Wall you build the nest cup from small pellets.

flow.do: Leave the nest upright in a dry place for one day. Then put three marbles in the cup, one at a time, and count to 60.
flow.say: It has dried for a day. Put the marbles in one at a time. Watch the place where the nest joins the cardboard.
flow.kid: Wait one day. Put in three marbles. Count to 60.
flow.wait: Let the nest dry for one day
flow.context: In this step of Stick a Nest to a Wall you test the dry nest with three marbles.

flow.do: Ask your child what held, what cracked and why. Then they change one thing for the second design in 'your turn'.
flow.say: Say what held and what cracked. Why do you think it cracked there? A swallow mixes grass into her mud. What might the grass do?
flow.kid: Say what held and what broke. What one thing will you change?

ask.q: Why might bits of grass in the mud help?
good: They hold the two sides of a crack together.
They tie the pellets to each other.

flow.think: A swallow makes about a thousand trips with mud for one nest. Why might she come back to the same nest next year?
flow.context: This is the last step of Stick a Nest to a Wall. You look at how your nest did and plan one change.

items.p: Which beak is best for cracking hard seeds?
items.why: A short, thick beak has its tip close to the hinge, so the bite is hard. Long beaks reach far, and bite weakly at the tip.

items.p: Where along a beak is the bite strongest?
items.why: A beak is a lever. The closing muscles pull near the hinge, so the bite is strongest there and weakest at the tip.

items.p: A foot with skin stretched between the toes is called a ____ foot.
items.why: A webbed foot pushes a lot of water, like a paddle. Ducks and geese have webbed feet.

items.p: A vulture needs sharp talons to get food.
items.why: False. A vulture eats animals who are already dead, so there is nothing to catch. Her claws are blunt and her feet are made for walking.

items.p: Match each kind of foot to what it does.
pairs: Long legs and long, bare toes
items.why: Ask what surface the foot meets and what it must hold. A twig, bark, water, mud and prey each need a different foot.

items.p: Sort these birds by beak: built for a hard bite, or built for a long reach?
items.why: Sparrows, munias and parakeets crack seeds. Godwits, sunbirds and storks reach into mud, flowers or water.

items.p: Why does a godwit leave Siberia in autumn?
opts: The mud freezes over her food
items.why: The worms are still in the ground, and a thin beak cannot enter frozen mud. She flies to places where the mud stays soft.

items.p: A nest is a home where a bird lives all year.
items.why: False. Most birds use a nest only while there are eggs and chicks. For the rest of the year they sleep on branches, ledges or water.

items.p: Put these in order, from longest ago to now.
items: Archaeopteryx flies in what is now Germany
a: Archaeopteryx flies in what is now Germany
items.why: The first dinosaurs lived about 230 million years ago, and Archaeopteryx about 150 million years ago. The asteroid struck 66 million years ago.

items.p: Birds belong to the group of two-legged dinosaurs called ____.
items.why: Theropods walked on two legs and had hollow bones, three main toes and a wishbone. Tyrannosaurus, Velociraptor and all birds are theropods.

items.p: Which feature do birds share with Velociraptor?
items.why: A Velociraptor wishbone has been found. Velociraptor also had teeth and a long bony tail, and birds have lost both.

items.p: A sunbird has a long, thin, curved beak. Explain in two sentences what this beak is for.
items.a: It reaches the nectar deep inside a flower, where a short thick beak could not go. The thin beak is weak at the tip, and nectar does not need a hard bite.
items.why: A strong answer links the shape to the job, and says that reach matters here and bite strength does not.

items.p: Scissors cut 16 layers near the hinge and 4 layers at the tips. What does that tell you about beaks?
items.a: A beak is hinged like scissors, so the bite is strong near the hinge and weak at the tip. A short beak bites hard, and a long beak has a weak tip.
items.why: A strong answer uses the numbers as evidence and moves from the scissors to a real beak.

items.p: Draw a nest for a tree where snakes climb. Label how your nest keeps the eggs safe.
items.a: Any nest that a snake cannot easily reach or enter. One example is a nest hanging from a thin branch tip with the door at the bottom. Another is a hole with a very narrow opening.
items.why: A strong drawing names the danger and shows one feature that deals with it. A baya weaver's hanging nest and a hornbill's sealed hole are two real answers.
items.art: A blank box with a tree trunk on the left and one long thin branch reaching to the right.

items.p: What does 'incubate' mean?
opts: Keep eggs warm until they hatch
items.why: A chick grows inside an egg only if the egg stays warm. Most birds incubate by sitting on the eggs.

worksheets.title: Read the body, find the food

items.p: A kingfisher's long beak bites weakly at the tip. What is that beak good at?
opts: Snapping shut fast on a fish
items.why: The tip of a long beak moves far and fast. A fish needs speed and reach, and does not need a hard bite.

items.p: A parakeet has two toes pointing forward and two back. What does this help her do?
items.why: Two toes each way make a strong grip on bark, and let one foot hold a fruit like a hand.

items.p: After a drought, finches had deeper beaks on average. Why?
opts: Deep-beaked finches lived and had chicks
Each finch stretched their own beak
items.why: Only big, hard seeds were left. Finches with deeper beaks could crack them, so more of them lived and passed deep beaks to their chicks.

items.p: Sinosauropteryx had feathers and could not fly. What does this show?
items.why: A dinosaur with short arms and a coat of feathers could not fly. So feathers first did another job, such as keeping the body warm.

items.p: In the Frozen Mud Test, the tweezers found no beans because the beans were gone.
items.why: False. All ten beans were still in the bowl. The mud was too hard for the tweezers to enter.

items.p: Winter visitors come to India to lay their eggs.
items.why: False. Winter visitors nest in the north during the northern summer. They come to India to feed while the north is frozen.

items.p: Sort these features: found in birds and in small theropods, or only in the old theropods?
items.why: Fossils show feathers, wishbones, hollow bones and nesting in small theropods. Birds alive today have no teeth and only a short tail stump.

items.p: Three of these birds are waders. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Godwits, storks and herons have long legs and feed in shallow water. A parakeet climbs trees and eats seeds and fruit.

items.p: Each fold doubles the layers of a newspaper stack. How many layers are there after 4 folds?
items.why: One fold gives 2 layers, two folds give 4, three give 8 and four give 16.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how a drought changed the finches' beaks.
items: The small, soft seeds are eaten up
Finches with deeper beaks crack the big, hard seeds
More deep-beaked finches live through the drought
Their chicks have deeper beaks too
a: The small, soft seeds are eaten up
Finches with deeper beaks crack the big, hard seeds
More deep-beaked finches live through the drought
Their chicks have deeper beaks too
items.why: No single finch changed. The drought changed which finches lived, and the chicks took after their parents.

items.p: A koel builds no nest. Explain how a koel's egg is still kept warm.
items.a: The female koel lays her egg in a crow's nest. The crows sit on it with their own eggs, and then feed the koel chick.
items.why: A strong answer says who does the incubating. It may add that the egg must look enough like a crow's egg to be accepted.

items.p: Why is a short, thick beak poor at getting nectar from a long flower?
items.a: The nectar lies deep inside the flower, further than a short beak can reach. A hard bite is no help, because nectar is a liquid.
items.why: A strong answer names reach as the problem. It shows that a beak that suits one food suits another badly.

items.p: A bird has long legs, long bare toes and a long straight beak. Where does this bird feed, and why?
items.a: On wet mud or in shallow water. Long legs keep the body dry, and long toes stop the bird sinking. The long beak reaches worms deep in the mud.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason from each of the three clues. Bare toes with no web show that the bird walks and does not paddle.

items.p: People disagree about whether to call a hen a dinosaur.

views.says: A hen sits on the theropod branch of the dinosaur family tree. If Velociraptor is a dinosaur, a hen must be one too.
Words are for being understood. Everyone uses 'dinosaur' for the giant animals who died out. Calling a hen a dinosaur confuses people.
Say 'birds are living dinosaurs'. It keeps the everyday word 'bird' and still tells the truth about the family.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about fossils. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that feathers, wishbones and nests place birds inside the theropod group. Another is that a word is useful only if people share its meaning.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer keeps the facts about the family tree apart from the question of which word to use.

items.p: Label three parts of this hen's leg: the toes, the ankle and the knee.
a: The toes: the only part that touches the ground
The ankle: the joint that points backward, held high off the ground
The knee: close to the body, hidden in the feathers
items.why: A hen stands on her toes. So the joint that looks like a backward knee is the ankle, and the real knee is higher up.
items.art: A side view of a hen's leg and foot with the feathers of the body drawn faintly, and three blank label lines.

items.p: A bird has a large hooked beak and weak feet with blunt claws. What does she most likely eat?
items.why: The hook tears meat, and weak feet with blunt claws cannot kill. This is the plan of a vulture.

items.p: Several wet years bring plenty of small, soft seeds. What may happen to finch beaks over the generations?
opts: Every finch gets the same beak
items.why: A big beak costs more to grow and is clumsy with small seeds. When small seeds are plentiful, finches with smaller beaks raise more chicks.

items.p: Gerhard Heilmann said dinosaurs had no wishbone, so birds could not come from them. What showed he was wrong?
items.why: Wishbones have been found in many theropods. Heilmann's reasoning was careful, and the fossils he needed had not yet been recognised.

items.p: Which is the best evidence that some dinosaurs sat on their eggs?
opts: A fossil dinosaur found on a nest
items.why: Fossils of Citipati show the animal sitting on the nest with the arms spread over the eggs. What hens do today is only a hint.

items.p: A crocodile is a closer relative of a sparrow than of a lizard.
items.why: True. Crocodiles and dinosaurs, including birds, share a more recent ancestor than the one that they share with lizards.

items.p: In a drought, each finch grows a deeper beak by cracking hard seeds.
items.why: False. A finch's beak depth is set once the bird is grown. The drought changed which finches lived.

items.p: Match each nest to the problem it solves.
pairs: A woven nest hanging from a branch tip
Speckled eggs in a scrape on stony ground
Hunters cannot easily see the eggs
A mud nest stuck under a bridge
Rain and climbing animals cannot reach it
A tree hole sealed up to a narrow slit
Nothing wider than a beak can get in
items.why: Every nest answers a danger in the place where it is built. The same bird in another place would need another answer.

items.p: Force × distance from the hinge is always 24. What is the force 6 cm from the hinge?
items.why: 24 divided by 6 is 4. At 2 centimetres the force would be 12, which is three times more. So the bite at 6 centimetres is three times weaker, because that place is three times as far from the hinge.

items.p: About 1,200 finches lived on an island. About 180 lived through a drought. How many did not?
items.why: 1,200 minus 180 is 1,020. More than 8 finches in every 10 died, so the few who lived shaped the next generation strongly.

items.p: The V-shaped bone made of two joined collarbones is called the ____.
items.why: Birds have a wishbone, and so did many theropods, including Velociraptor and Tyrannosaurus.

items.p: Many people say, 'The dinosaurs died out.' Rewrite the sentence so that it is true, and explain your change.
items.a: One true sentence is this. All the dinosaurs except birds died out about 66 million years ago. Birds are theropod dinosaurs, and more than 10,000 kinds are alive.
items.why: A strong answer keeps what is right in the old sentence and adds the one exception, with a reason.

items.p: A fossil beak is short and thick. What does this show about the food, and what does it not show?
items.a: It shows that the beak could bite hard, so the animal could crack hard food such as seeds. It does not show what the animal really chose to eat each day, or how they behaved.
items.why: A strong answer separates what the shape allows from what the animal did. A beak shows what was possible.

items.p: The Frozen Mud Test used beans as worms. How is a bean unlike a worm? Does that change the result?
items.a: A worm can move and a bean cannot, and a worm is soft. It does not change the main result, because tweezers could not enter frozen mud at all.
items.why: A strong answer names a real difference and then judges whether that difference could change the finding.

items.p: Each October, huge flocks of Amur falcons rest near a village in Nagaland on their way to Africa.

views.who: A villager who used to trap the falcons
views.says: October is a hard month for us. The falcons came in thousands, and selling them fed my family.
These falcons fly from East Asia to southern Africa. Birds caught here are lost to every country on the route.
We stopped the trapping, and visitors now pay to see the falcons. That money must reach the families who gave up trapping.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about migration. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that a migrating bird depends on every resting place along the route. Another is that people who protect the birds must also be able to live.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses the fact that one resting place serves birds from a whole continent. It also takes the villagers' needs seriously.

items.p: Draw a beak for a bird who eats water snails with hard, round shells. Label two features.
items.a: One good design is a long beak that reaches into shallow water. The beak also needs a way to hold a round shell, such as a gap or a strong tip. Each label says what the feature does.
items.why: A strong drawing deals with both problems: reaching the snail and holding the slippery shell. The Asian openbill, a stork, has a gap between the two halves of the beak.
items.art: A blank box with a round snail shell drawn under a wavy water line.

quiz.p: A bird has a flat, wide beak with edges like a comb. How does she feed?
quiz.why: The comb-like edges let water out and keep small food in. Ducks feed this way.

quiz.p: Why can a sparrow crack a seed that a godwit cannot?
opts: Her beak tip is close to the hinge
A godwit has no jaw muscles
quiz.why: A short beak keeps the tip near the hinge, where the bite is strong. The tip of a godwit's long beak is far from the hinge.

quiz.p: In the Beak Lever Test, where did the scissor blades open widest?
quiz.why: The tips are farthest from the hinge, so they travel farthest. That is why a long beak reaches far and snaps fast.

quiz.p: Which feet belong to a bird who catches live prey?
quiz.why: Talons grip and kill. Webbed feet paddle, long thin toes spread weight on mud, and thick blunt claws scratch the ground.

quiz.p: Why does a jacana have very long toes?
opts: To spread her weight on floating leaves
quiz.why: Long toes spread her weight over a wide area, so a floating leaf can hold her up.

quiz.p: Why does a baya weaver hang the nest from a thin branch tip?
quiz.why: A thin tip will not hold a climbing hunter, and the entrance points down. The nest answers the danger of that place.

quiz.p: Every kind of bird builds a nest of their own.
quiz.why: False. A koel lays her egg in a crow's nest, and a lapwing lays on almost bare ground.

quiz.p: Why do godwits spend the winter in India?
opts: Northern mud freezes, and Indian mud stays soft
They come here to lay eggs
quiz.why: A godwit feeds by probing mud. When the northern ground freezes, the food is locked away, so she flies to soft mud.

quiz.p: Which of these birds is a winter visitor to India?
quiz.why: Bar-headed geese nest in Mongolia and Tibet and fly to India for the winter. Crows, mynas and parakeets live here all year.

quiz.p: Which group of dinosaurs do birds belong to?
opts: Theropods, who walked on two legs
quiz.why: Theropods had hollow bones, three main toes and a wishbone. Small feathered theropods were the ancestors of birds.

quiz.p: A fossil found in 1996 showed a small dinosaur with a coat of feathers. Why did that matter?
opts: It was strong evidence that birds are dinosaurs
It proved all dinosaurs could fly
quiz.why: Before 1996, feathers were known only on birds. A feathered dinosaur who could not fly tied the two groups together.

quiz.p: After a drought, finches had deeper beaks on average. What had changed?
quiz.why: Natural selection changes the mix of individuals in a group. No finch's own beak grew deeper.

applications: Tool makers use the same lever rule that beaks follow. Pliers for cutting thick wire have short jaws close to the hinge. Tweezers and long-nosed pliers have long jaws for reaching.
Scientists who rebuild dinosaurs look at living birds. A hen's bones, eggs and nesting help them work out how Velociraptor grew, bred and moved.
People who protect wetlands use rings and trackers on migrating birds. The routes show which marshes in India must be kept wet for birds from Siberia.
The villagers of Pangti in Nagaland once trapped Amur falcons. Since 2013 they have guarded the resting flocks, after local people such as the journalist Bano Haralu reported the trapping.
Farmers welcome barn owls, because one owl family eats hundreds of rats in a year. The talons and hooked beak show what the owl is good at.
Bird rescuers read the beak and feet of a tired bird. This tells them what kind of place to let the bird go in.

open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think small feathered dinosaurs glided down from trees. Others think they ran and leapt from the ground, or flapped to climb slopes. Fossils have not settled it.

open_questions.q: How does a migrating bird sense the Earth's magnetic field?
open_questions.why_open: One idea is that a chemical in the eye responds to the field. Another is that tiny grains of iron in the beak do. Tests have not settled which is right.

open_questions.q: Why did only some birds live through the asteroid strike?
open_questions.why_open: Small size, seed-eating and living on the ground may each have helped. Very few bird fossils are known from just after the strike.

open_questions.q: How much does a sleeping bird rely on the lock in the toe tendons?
open_questions.why_open: The lock is there, but tests on starlings found sleeping birds standing with loose toes. Few kinds of bird have been tested.
Colour grains have been found in only a few feathered fossils. For most dinosaurs, including Tyrannosaurus, nobody knows.

maths.problem: In one Beak Lever Test, the scissors cut 16 layers near the hinge. They cut 8 in the middle and 4 at the tips. The three places were 2, 4 and 8 centimetres from the screw. What happens to the layers each time the distance doubles?
maths.answer: Each time the distance doubles, the number of layers halves.
maths.explain: From 2 to 4 centimetres, the layers fall from 16 to 8. From 4 to 8 centimetres, they fall from 8 to 4. Double the distance gives half the cut.
maths.context: In the Beak Lever Test you cut stacks of newspaper with scissors at three places along the blades. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern turns three separate results into one rule about levers.

maths.problem: For one beak, the bite force multiplied by the distance from the hinge is always 24. Find the force at 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 centimetres from the hinge. At which of these distances is the force more than 5?
maths.answer: The forces are 12, 8, 6, 4 and 3. The force is more than 5 at 2, 3 and 4 centimetres.
maths.explain: 24 divided by 2 is 12. 24 divided by 3 is 8. 24 divided by 4 is 6. 24 divided by 6 is 4. 24 divided by 8 is 3. So a seed that needs a force of 5 can be cracked only within 4 centimetres of the hinge.
maths.context: The Beak Lever Test showed that scissors cut hardest near the hinge. A beak follows the same lever rule, and here the rule is given in numbers.
maths.why_maths: Dividing shows exactly how far along a beak a hard seed can still be cracked.

maths.problem: About 1,200 finches lived on Daphne Major before the 1977 drought. About 180 lived through it. About how many finches out of every 20 lived?
maths.explain: 1,200 divided by 20 is 60, so the flock is 60 groups of 20. 180 divided by 60 is 3. So about 3 finches in every 20 lived, and about 17 in every 20 died.
maths.context: Rosemary and Peter Grant counted and measured the finches on a small island called Daphne Major. A drought in 1977 killed most of the finches.
maths.why_maths: A share out of 20 is easier to picture than two big numbers. It shows how hard the drought pressed on the finches.

maths.problem: A wader flies 60 kilometres every hour for 8 hours each night. Her winter marsh is 4,800 kilometres away. How many nights of flying does she need? If she rests for 2 days after every 2 nights of flying, how long is the whole journey?
maths.answer: 10 nights of flying. With the rests, the journey takes 18 days.
maths.explain: 60 times 8 is 480 kilometres each night. 4,800 divided by 480 is 10 nights. Ten nights are five pairs of nights. She rests after the first four pairs, which is 4 rests of 2 days, or 8 days. 10 plus 8 is 18 days.
maths.context: Godwits and other waders fly from Central Asia and Siberia to India each autumn. The speed and the distance here are made-up round numbers of about the right size.
maths.why_maths: Working out the nights and the rests shows why a migrating bird needs safe marshes along the whole route.

maths.problem: In one Frozen Mud Test, the tweezers found 9 beans in soft mud. In the frozen bowl they found 0 at the start, 2 after 20 minutes and 6 after 40 minutes. If the thawing goes on in the same way, about when will the count reach 9? Why can you not be sure?
maths.answer: At about 55 to 60 minutes. You cannot be sure, because the count did not rise by the same amount each time.
maths.explain: The count rose by 2 in the first 20 minutes and by 4 in the next 20. Three more beans are needed. At 4 or more beans every 20 minutes, that takes about 15 minutes more. The speed of thawing is changing, so this is an estimate.
maths.context: In the Frozen Mud Test you search a frozen bowl of mud for hidden beans while the mud thaws. These are made-up counts.
maths.why_maths: Looking at how fast the count rises lets you predict when frozen ground becomes a feeding place again.

maths.problem: Birds first flew about 150 million years ago. The asteroid struck 66 million years ago. For how many million years did birds live beside the other dinosaurs? Our own kind of human is about 300,000 years old. How many times longer is that shared time?
maths.answer: 84 million years. That is 280 times as long as our kind of human has existed.
maths.explain: 150 minus 66 is 84 million years. 84 million divided by 300,000 is the same as 840 divided by 3, which is 280.
maths.context: In the project From Crocodile to Sparrow you put Archaeopteryx, Tyrannosaurus, a hen and a sparrow on one family tree. This problem compares their times.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two lengths of time shows how long birds and other dinosaurs shared the Earth.

founder: Founder's notebook for The world of birds: the evolution picture book, whose timeline has dinosaurs from about 230 million years ago, birds from dinosaurs about 150 million years ago, and the dinosaur extinction 66 million years ago. Its introduction says that evolution is a branching tree in which every kind keeps changing. That idea shapes the family tree project and the section on finch beaks.

The Combined Class 4 lesson sci-C4-the-world-of-birds was read. Its story, its drought game and its feather, wing and egg activities are not reused. Flight, feathers and eggs are left to sci.forces.flight and sci.animals.animal-life-cycles.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1861, quarry workers in Germany found a fossil with feathered wings, teeth and a long bony tail. The animal was named Archaeopteryx. In 1868 the English scientist Thomas Huxley compared the bones with those of small dinosaurs. He said that birds had come from dinosaurs. In 1926 the Danish artist Gerhard Heilmann wrote a careful book that disagreed. Birds have a wishbone, which is made of two collarbones. No dinosaur seemed to have collarbones. Heilmann reasoned that a lost bone could not come back, so birds must have come from older reptiles. For about forty years most scientists agreed with him. Then, in 1964, John Ostrom found a quick hunting dinosaur in Montana, in America, and named it Deinonychus. The wrist and hand were built like a bird's. Wishbones were later found in many theropods. In 1996 a farmer named Li Yumin found Sinosauropteryx in Liaoning, in China. The fossil showed a small dinosaur with a coat of feathers. Since then, dozens of kinds of feathered dinosaur have been found.
how_we_found_out.who: Thomas Huxley in England, Gerhard Heilmann in Denmark, John Ostrom in America, and Li Yumin, Ji Qiang and Ji Shu'an in China
how_we_found_out.when: Archaeopteryx was found in 1861. Huxley wrote in 1868 and Heilmann in 1926. Ostrom found Deinonychus in 1964, and Sinosauropteryx was found in 1996.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That birds could not have come from dinosaurs, because dinosaurs had no wishbone. Wishbones were later found in many theropods, and feathered dinosaurs were found from 1996.
